claims.h2: Claims, and how each one is checked
claims.intro: A claim without a check is a hope. The right-hand column says which is which.
claims.caption: Accessibility claims for this website

rows.claim: Colour contrast meets the ratios stated below
rows.how: Measured on every build by scripts/check-contrast.mjs against the design tokens; the build fails below the declared minimum.
Measured by scripts/check-i18n.mjs, which fails on a bare literal in a text position or in aria-label, alt, title or placeholder.
Reviewed by hand, not automated. Written as real header, nav, main and footer elements with accessible names.
Reviewed by hand in Safari and Chrome on macOS. Not automated.
A prefers-reduced-motion rule in the stylesheet removes transitions and smooth scrolling. Not automated.
Not done. Written here as not done rather than left out.

contrast.body: Body text must reach at least {body}:1 against its background, links at least {link}:1 and secondary text at least {muted}:1. The crimson accent measures 4.27:1 on the dark background: enough for rules, borders and large display type, not enough for body text. So it is never used for body text, and a lighter crimson at 7.40:1 carries the links.
contrast.gate: Those minimums are read from the same file the gate reads, so this page cannot claim a ratio the build does not enforce. Run it yourself:

items: A skip link is the first focusable element on every page and becomes visible when it takes focus.
Focus is always visible: a two-pixel outline in a colour measured against both themes.
The theme control is a button, reached with Tab and operated with Enter or Space.
The ticket composer is an ordinary form. Every field has a label, and the result is a link you follow deliberately, never an automatic submission.
Nothing traps focus. There are no modal dialogs, carousels or infinite scrolls on this site.

motion.body: There are no animations, no autoplaying media and no parallax. Smooth scrolling is the only motion the stylesheet asks for, and prefers-reduced-motion removes it outright, along with every transition, rather than merely shortening them.

landmarks.intro: The page skeleton is the same everywhere:
items: One h1 per page, then h2 sections in document order. No heading level is skipped for a visual effect.
header, nav, main and footer are real elements, and every nav has an accessible name, so a screen reader can tell the main navigation from the language switcher and from the footer groups.
Tables have a caption and row or column headers. They are never used for layout.
The page language is declared with a full BCP-47 tag, and each language link declares the language it leads to.
No screen-reader pass has been done with NVDA, JAWS or VoiceOver.
No automated audit (axe, Lighthouse, pa11y) is wired into the build yet.
Contrast is measured between design tokens, not against rendered pixels, so an inherited colour somewhere could still be wrong.
The site has not been tested at 200% zoom or with a browser text-size override on a small screen.
Polish and English are the only locales. No right-to-left language has been laid out, although the stylesheet uses logical properties where it matters.

feedback.body: Open a documentation ticket saying what you were trying to do, what you used and what happened. An accessibility barrier is a defect, not a feature request.

home.h1: A hardened downstream distribution of Redox OS
home.paragraph: E-OS is a distribution of Redox OS, a Unix-like operating system whose microkernel is written in Rust. It is not written from scratch: the kernel, the C library, the filesystem and the driver stack come from Redox, and E-OS adds a verified boot chain, a package index signed with a hybrid ed25519 + ML-DSA-65 signature, a per-user kernel-scheme allowlist and a curated desktop. It is also not finished. The x86_64 image currently ships with no active package source, so a fix released today cannot reach an installed x86_64 system through the update mechanism; the browser in the image is an upstream prebuilt rather than the hardened build its recipe describes; and it is a single-maintainer project. Everything on this site that says something was measured names what was measured and when.

verified.intro: Each row was checked against a built artefact — an image that was mounted, an index that was verified, a machine that reached a login prompt — not against the source that was supposed to produce it.
verified.caption: Verified properties, with the measurement behind each

rows.measured: The bootloader authenticates the kernel and the initfs with ed25519 over SHA-512(role, length, data) before the magic-byte check and before any byte is used. A missing signature or a zero key refuses to boot, and domain separation means a signed initfs cannot verify as a kernel.
repo.toml carries a hybrid ed25519 + ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204) signature. Checked against the live aarch64 index of 79 packages: both halves verify, and one flipped byte makes both refuse.

rows.what: Package bytes bound to the signed index
rows.measured: The blake3 digest from the authenticated manifest is checked against the bytes about to be extracted, on every install path including pkg install. The serial and expires fields give rollback and freeze protection.

Both UEFI bootloaders carry SBAT and are Authenticode-signed, with SBAT stamped before signing because Authenticode covers the whole file. The installation medium carries the E-OS certificate as DER at EFI/EOS/eos-secureboot.der, because a firmware menu is where it is needed.
boot-smoke reached userspace login on x86_64 and on aarch64, exit 0, measured 2026-09-01.

Partition, install, reboot, login proven once and re-proven after the shared-interrupt fix. The encrypted path is exercised with a deliberately wrong password that has to fail before the correct one is allowed to work.
/etc/login_schemes.toml grants root everything and the unprivileged account an explicit 25-scheme list. Raw IP sockets are removed from that list.
16 drivers run as ordinary processes, so a driver fault does not take the kernel down. Without an IOMMU this is process isolation, not hardware isolation, and the roadmap says so.
RedoxFS AES-XTS, offered by the installer. Hardware-accelerated on aarch64 through the ARMv8 crypto extensions; a software path on x86_64.
The text login and the graphical greeter both refuse to continue while the account has no password.

limits.intro: The same page has to carry both halves, or the first half is advertising.
items: The x86_64 image ships with no active package source: both entries in /etc/pkg.d/ are commented out, so an update cannot reach an installed x86_64 system.
The browser in the image is the upstream NetSurf 3.11 prebuilt, not the position-independent build its recipe describes — readelf reports type EXEC at 0x400000, measured 2026-09-02.

Passwords set in the running system are hashed with argon2i at m=4096, t=3 — 4.0 ms per guess against the 14.1 ms of the argon2id used at image-build time. Two paths, and the stronger one is not the one a user gets.
A reproducible build has not been demonstrated. The same commit has never been shown to produce the same image byte for byte.
Nothing has been verified on physical hardware. QEMU does not prove that firmware will boot the medium or that a driver will bind a real chipset.
There is no ISO release, no cosign signature and no published PGP key. Release artefacts carry a minisign signature over SHA256SUMS.
The desktop applications have no automated tests at all, and no host window backend, so they type-check off Redox but do not open a window there.
It is a single-maintainer project. That matters when deciding how much to depend on it.

products.body: {shipped} products are in the image today and {planned} more are roadmap rows with an estimate — decisions, not code.

repos.body: Thirty repositories in one manifest, each pinned by revision. Four kinds: components written for E-OS, read-only mirrors of upstream Redox, forks carrying E-OS patches, and published package artefacts.

changelog.body: Every changelog entry names the commit that introduced it and what was measured, so any line can be checked. This site parses that file at build time instead of retyping it.

upstream.body: Substantial parts of E-OS — the kernel, relibc, RedoxFS, the driver stack and the cookbook build system — come from Redox OS and remain under the MIT licence. E-OS is an independent downstream distribution: it is not official Redox OS software and it is not endorsed by the Redox OS nonprofit.

products.lede: What ships in the image today, what is a roadmap row, and what the difference is. This list is generated from the build configuration, not written by hand.

generated.body: The entries below are built from the package tables and the repository manifest in the E-OS orchestration repository. Three hand-written product lists in this project have already drifted apart from the configuration; that is why roadmap row PR-001 exists and why this page has a generator instead of a paragraph.

shipped.intro: Each of these has a package entry in the build configuration. Where a first-party repository exists, the pinned revision below is the one the image is built from.

planned.intro: These four are decisions with a size estimate, not code. The repositories were created on 2026-09-03; at the time this page was written none of them carried a skeleton, a recipe or a pin.
planned.state: A roadmap row only: no repository content, no recipe, no package.

eos-notes.summary: A notes application for the Crimson desktop, written in Rust with Slint on the shared eos-ui backend.
eos-notes.detail: It stores notes in SQLite in write-ahead-log mode. It is a first-party E-OS component and is pinned by revision in its build recipe.

eos-control.summary: The control centre: system overview, processes, security, storage, power, sound and live network state.
eos-control.detail: It absorbed the standalone system monitor and the file-integrity monitor. The Security tab carries the blake3 baseline and the permission audit that used to live in a separate application.

eos-guard.summary: A file-integrity and permission monitor for the Crimson desktop, shipped as an application again since the owner's decision of 2026-09-03.
eos-guard.detail: It keeps a blake3 baseline of the files it watches and reports permission changes. The same engine also runs inside the Security tab of the control centre, from a second copy of the code rather than one shared library — recorded as debt on the roadmap, not hidden.

netsurf.summary: The web browser in the image: NetSurf 3.11.
netsurf.detail: The recipe builds it from source as a position-independent executable. The artefact currently in the image is not that build, and the roadmap tracks the difference rather than hiding it.

cosmic-term.summary: The terminal emulator, from the upstream COSMIC application set.
cosmic-term.detail: It is packaged and shipped unchanged; the editor and file manager come from the same set. E-OS does not maintain them and does not claim to.

eos-sheets.summary: A spreadsheet: cells, a small formula engine, CSV and TSV import and export.
eos-sheets.detail: The plan names roughly forty functions and a documented container format for a first version, with xlsx import later and no macro language at all.

eos-slides.summary: A presentation editor: a slide list, text and image boxes, and a presenter view on a second window.
eos-slides.detail: PDF export is planned through an existing Rust library. Importing pptx is explicitly not promised.

eos-drive.summary: A cloud drive: a WebDAV server on the E-OS server edition, and a sync client.
eos-drive.detail: It waits on a server edition that has never been built here, which makes it the furthest away of the four.

eos-store.summary: An application store over the package index that already exists and is already signed.
eos-store.detail: The index and the package tool exist. The metadata schema, the screenshots and the client interface do not. No accounts and no payments in a first version.

caveat.no-host-backend: No host window backend yet: it type-checks on macOS and Linux but does not open a window there.
caveat.no-tests: No automated tests in the repository yet, and therefore no coverage floor.
caveat.netsurf-prebuilt: Shipped as the upstream prebuilt binary, not as the hardened build the recipe describes — measured 2026-09-02.
caveat.not-started: Nothing is written. The row exists on the roadmap with a size estimate.
caveat.needs-server: Blocked on the E-OS server edition, which has never been built here.
caveat.duplicate-engine: The integrity engine exists twice — in this application and inside the control centre. Merging them into one library is roadmap row PR-004.
caveat.no-signature-engine: No signature scanning and no on-access hook. The word "antivirus" is not used for it until such an engine exists (roadmap rows PR-003 and PR-004b).

absent.intro: Two of these are choices with reasons and two are gaps the roadmap tracks. The project's own README blurred that distinction once and had to correct it; the distinction is kept here.
items: No antivirus. The word is not used until an on-access engine exists. The security product is E-OS Guard, which does integrity and permission monitoring.
No mandatory access control of the SELinux or AppArmor kind. The access-control model is the per-user kernel-scheme allowlist.
No backup tool. That is a gap, and the roadmap tracks it as such.
No VPN and no Tor. Also gaps: both are new subsystems, not a switch waiting to be flipped.
absent.link: The roadmap rows behind this list

about.lede: What this project is, who runs it, and the rules it holds itself to.

what.p1: E-OS is a distribution of Redox OS with a trust chain added: verified boot, a hybrid-signed package index, a curated desktop. The operating system itself is Redox — the kernel, the C library, the filesystem and the drivers come from upstream, some of them through forks that carry E-OS patches and are kept rebasable.
what.p2: It is not Tails, not Qubes OS and not GrapheneOS. Those solve different problems, and comparing E-OS with them would be unfair to a reader trying to choose. The comparison that makes sense is with Redox itself: E-OS is Redox with a chain of trust that can be checked.

repos.intro: Thirty repositories in one manifest, each pinned by revision. GitLab is the source of truth and GitHub is a read-only mirror. Mistaking one repository type for another is the most expensive mistake available in this project, so the type is a field that continuous integration enforces, not a sentence in a document.
repos.caption: Repository types, from the manifest

rows.meaning: Read-only vendored mirrors of upstream Redox, never hand-edited
Forks carrying E-OS patches, kept rebasable

who.p1: One maintainer. That is stated in the security policy too, because it is information a person needs when deciding how to disclose a vulnerability, or how much to depend on the project.
who.p2: There is no company behind E-OS, no legal entity and no funding. The copyright line reads "Damian (Gh0s777tt) and the E-OS contributors", and the whole is licensed under AGPL-3.0-or-later.

method.h2: The rules this project holds itself to
method.intro: These are not aspirations. Each of them exists because its absence broke something that then had to be found the hard way.
rules: A check that cannot fail is not a check. Every gate carries a negative test that has been seen going red.
Verify the artefact, not the exit code. A green build has repeatedly meant a binary that was two months old.
Fail closed by default. An exception needs an explicit environment variable, and the summary says what it skipped.
Measure, do not infer. A conclusion drawn from one directory is not a conclusion about every source.
Correct your own published conclusions in the open, with the correction next to what it replaces.
Documentation changes in the same merge request as the thing it documents, never in the next one.

notclaims.h2: What this project does not claim
notclaims.intro: Stated here so that nobody has to work it out from what is missing.
items: It does not claim to have been audited by anyone outside the project.
It does not claim reproducible builds. That is a goal; the comparison has not been run.
It does not claim to run on your hardware. Nothing has been booted on a physical machine yet.
It does not claim compatibility with Linux binaries or a stable syscall surface. The ABI is inherited from Redox and still moves.
It does not claim endorsement by the Redox OS project.

build.intro: The build runs in a container. On the reference host — Apple Silicon macOS with podman — the project directory sits on exFAT, which podman will not mount, so the wrapper builds inside a volume instead. These are the commands that were run, not a summary of them.
build.note: Running make directly from the project directory does not work on that host, and make will report that there is nothing to be done while assembling an image from stale artefacts. The wrapper exists for exactly that reason.

gates.intro: What can go red, and where.
gates.caption: Gates in the orchestration repository

rows.state: Sixteen stages. Exit 1 means a defect was found; exit 2 means the gate could not run. A missing scanner is exit 2, never a pass.
Eighteen invariant checks, plus a probe that checks its own instruments before the first check runs.
Boots the built image in QEMU and waits for a userspace login prompt. PASS on both architectures, measured 2026-09-01.
Secret scanning over the full history, and advisory scanning on both manifests.
cargo llvm-cov with a floor of 38% of lines on the signing tool; 41.06% measured on 2026-09-01. The floor catches regression, it does not certify 38% as a good number.
Errors block, warnings are advisory. Zero errors across the shell scripts.

gates.ci: GitLab shared runners are quota-limited and run out intermittently. GitHub Actions has never produced a run for this repository. The self-hosted eos-heavy runner spends no shared minutes and is what the heavy jobs use — including this website's pages job. A local run of verify.sh is the only gate known in advance to execute.

contribute.intro: The short version of the contract:
rules: No commits on main. Branch, then a merge request.
No force-push, ever, including on your own branch.
One logical change per merge request.
Every change has a test, or a written reason why a test is impossible, agreed before the change lands.
Never hand-edit a generated file — the lockfiles, the SBOMs, the third-party licence list. Regenerate them.
No secrets in the repository or in a log. Generating a signing key is a human action and is deliberately not automated.

site.intro: The site is a separate repository with static output and no backend. Its own gates run before the build:
site.note: check-i18n fails when a key is missing from a catalogue or when a component carries a bare string in a text position. check-changelog fails when the parser regresses or when the vendored changelog drifts from the orchestration repository. check-contrast measures every colour pair the accessibility statement claims. All three exit 1 for a finding and 2 when they could not run at all.

changelog.lede: Parsed at build time from CHANGELOG.md in the orchestration repository. Nothing here is retyped, so the site and the record cannot disagree.

language.body: The entries are reproduced exactly as they were written, and many of them are in Polish. Translating them here would create a second version of a record whose value is that it is the original. The page around them follows your language choice; the record does not.

changelog.provenance: Source: {origin} · {bytes} bytes · sha256 {sha} · CRLF {crlf} · {releases} releases · {sections} sections · {entries} entries
changelog.sourceLink: The file this page was built from

downloads.lede: Developer-only for now. This page says what that means on a static host, and what it cannot mean.

gate.p1: The owner's decision on 2026-09-03 was that downloads stay closed to developers until further notice. This site is served by GitLab Pages, which serves files and runs nothing: it cannot ask who you are, so it cannot enforce a gate.
gate.p2: So the gate is not a switch that hides links from you. It is the absence of the links: while the flag below is true, no artefact URL is written into this page at all. A client-side "are you a developer?" toggle would be decoration, and this page will not pretend otherwise. A real gate needs the server-side identity service that is still a roadmap row.

closed.h2: There are no download links on this page
closed.body: Deliberately. The reasons are worth stating, because they are also the reasons the flag has not flipped yet:
reasons: Nothing has been booted on physical hardware. Publishing an image implies it is meant to be run on a machine that has never been tested.
The x86_64 image ships with no active package source, so an installed system cannot receive a fix through the update mechanism.
There is no ISO and no cosign signature. Release artefacts carry a minisign signature over a SHA256SUMS file.
A real download gate needs a server-side identity check, and that does not exist yet.
closed.buildBody: The build is reproducible in the sense of "it runs", not yet in the sense of "byte for byte". It needs podman and roughly 37 GB of build cache.

existing.intro: Honesty requires saying that some things are downloadable today, even though this page publishes nothing:
items: The signed aarch64 package index is public on GitHub Pages and answers with HTTP 200. The x86_64 index answers 404.
Nightly images exist as continuous-integration job artefacts with a one-week retention.
A GitHub release object exists for v0.1.0 only. v0.2.0 is an annotated, signed tag with no release object behind it.

verify.h2: If you do get an image, verify it
verify.intro: The steps that matter, in order:
steps: Check the SHA256SUMS file against the raw image, not against the compressed transport wrapper.
Verify the minisign signature over SHA256SUMS with the published public key before trusting any digest in it.
If you boot under Secure Boot on a machine that is not yours to reconfigure, expect to enrol the E-OS certificate first. It travels on the installation medium at EFI/EOS/eos-secureboot.der.
After installation, check that the trust anchors under /etc/pkg/ match the published public halves.

hardware.body: The compatibility matrix lists what has been booted and what has not. Everything marked as needing physical hardware is unverified: QEMU does not prove that firmware will boot the medium, or that a driver will bind a real chipset.

support.lede: A FAQ, a ticket that becomes a GitLab issue, and an AI assistant that is designed and not built.

security.h3: Security bugs do not go here
security.body: Do not open a public ticket for a vulnerability. There are two private channels and both are monitored.
security.link: How to report a security problem

tickets.p1: There is no backend. This site is static files on GitLab Pages, so a form on this page cannot store anything and cannot send anything.
tickets.p2: A ticket is therefore an issue in a GitLab project. The form below composes a prefilled "new issue" link inside your browser. Nothing leaves this page until you follow that link, and GitLab is where you review the text and submit it. You need a GitLab account to do so.

items: Tickets are public. Anything you paste into one is public from the moment it is submitted.
You need a GitLab account. There is no anonymous ticket.
There is no ticket number until GitLab creates one, and this site sends no email.
A very long description does not survive a URL. The composer tells you when the link gets too long; paste the rest into the issue after it opens.
Nothing on this page is stored, so a half-written ticket is lost if you close the tab.

ticket.noBackend: Nothing here is transmitted. The button below opens GitLab with the fields already filled in.

categories.label: Bug
categories.hint: Something behaves differently from what is documented.

categories.label: Question
categories.hint: You could not find the answer in the documentation.

categories.label: Hardware report
categories.hint: It booted, or it did not, on a specific machine.

categories.label: Documentation
categories.hint: Something on this site or in the documents is wrong or missing.

ticket.open: Open the prefilled ticket on GitLab
ticket.ready: Link ready. Review it on GitLab before submitting. Length:
ticket.tooLong: The link is longer than GitLab accepts reliably. Shorten the text here and paste the rest after the issue opens.
ticket.needTitle: Add a summary to build the link.

nojs.body: These links work with scripting disabled. They carry the issue template only; you type the rest on GitLab.

ai.p1: There is no chat on this page and no endpoint behind it. Nothing you type anywhere on this site reaches a model.
ai.p2: The decision, taken on 2026-09-03, is that if E-OS ever has a support assistant then it runs its own model on its own machine. Calling somebody else's hosted service to answer questions about an operating system built around a verifiable trust chain would contradict the premise.
ai.p3: That has a cost, and the cost is why this is a design rather than a feature: E-OS has no GPU driver stack, no linear-algebra library in the image and no server edition that has ever been built. The design document says what a CPU-only Rust host can realistically run and what it cannot.

items: A model class that fits a CPU-only host: a one-to-four-billion-parameter instruction-tuned model, quantised, answering from retrieved documentation rather than from memory.
Retrieval over the documentation, the changelog and the roadmap, with every answer citing the file it came from.
Guardrails: no shell, no filesystem, no ticket creation, and a refusal path for when retrieval finds nothing.
Phases with sizes, so that the first phase is useful before the server edition exists.
It will not be a wrapper around somebody else's hosted model.
It will not answer security questions or triage vulnerabilities.
It will not act on your system or open tickets on your behalf.
It will not exist at all until the E-OS server edition does.

items.a: You can build it and run it in QEMU. Nothing has been booted on physical hardware yet, and the downloads page publishes no images.
No. It is a downstream distribution of Redox OS, whose microkernel is written in Rust. Linux binaries do not run on it.
x86_64 and aarch64. Both reached a userspace login prompt in QEMU on 2026-09-01.
On aarch64 the signed package index is live. On x86_64 the image has no active package source, which is tracked as an open defect rather than hidden.
No. It is a single-maintainer project with no legal entity behind it.

items.q: Why is the changelog partly in Polish?
items.a: Because it was written in Polish, and rewriting a record after the fact would make it less trustworthy rather than more. The page furniture is translated; the record is not.

items.q: How do I report that it does not boot on my machine?
items.a: Open a hardware report with the machine, the firmware, the architecture and the last line you saw. A photograph of the screen is more useful than a description of it.

items.q: Where do the roadmap identifiers this site keeps quoting come from?
items.a: From ROADMAP.md in the orchestration repository. Every identifier there carries a size estimate and, where the status says done, the evidence for it.

channels.intro: There are three, and none of them is a chat room.
channels.tickets: Tickets — issues in the support project
channels.response: The response targets are the ones in the security policy: 72 hours to acknowledge, seven days to an initial assessment. They are targets from one maintainer, not a contract.

security.lede: How to report a vulnerability, what the trust chain actually does, where it does not reach, and what this website knows about you.

report.p1: Do not open a public issue. Two private channels, both monitored:

targets.caveat: One caveat has to be stated plainly: the x86_64 image ships with no active package source, so a fix released today cannot reach an installed x86_64 system through the update mechanism.

chain.intro: Each of these was checked against a built artefact, not against the source that was supposed to produce it.
items: The bootloader verifies the kernel and the initfs by ed25519 signature before the magic-byte check and before any byte is used. Domain separation means a signed initfs cannot verify as a kernel.
The package index is signed with a hybrid ed25519 and ML-DSA-65 signature. Both halves must verify, and a single flipped byte makes both refuse.
The trust anchors are pinned inside the image and are byte-identical to the committed public halves.
Package bytes are checked against the blake3 digest in the authenticated manifest before extraction, with serial and expiry fields for rollback and freeze protection.
Both UEFI bootloaders carry SBAT and are Authenticode-signed, with SBAT stamped before signing because the signature covers the whole file.

gaps.intro: A trust chain that is only described is not a trust chain. These are the parts that are described but not yet true.
items: No IOMMU. Drivers are separate processes, which is process isolation, not hardware isolation.
Application sandboxing is planned, not shipped: the containment package is disabled and per-application policy does not exist.
There is no persistent audit log and no packet filter.
Passwords set in the running system are hashed with argon2i at m=4096, t=3 — weaker than the argon2id used when the image is built.
Signing keys live on the build host, not in a hardware security module or on a token. Key custody is a roadmap row blocked on hardware.
Nothing has been verified on physical hardware, so the boot chain is proven under QEMU and its firmware only.

sitedata.h2: What this website knows about you
sitedata.p1: Nothing that reaches the project. This site is static files with no analytics, no cookies, no trackers and no third-party fonts or scripts. The only browser storage it uses is a single localStorage entry holding your light or dark preference, which never leaves your device.
sitedata.p2: The host that serves the files sees your request the way any web server does, under its own operator's policy. If you follow a link to GitLab, GitHub or Redox OS, their policies apply from that point onwards.

items.a: Not by anyone outside the project. There are internal audit reports in the repository with dates and methods; they are self-assessments and say so.
The package index signature is hybrid ed25519 and ML-DSA-65, so that one surface is. Nothing else in the system is, and the phrase should not be applied to E-OS as a whole.
Not by construction. Access depends on the kernel scheme capability set rather than on the user id, which was measured by watching sudo and root fail identically on a denied scheme.
No. There is no funding behind the project.

items.q: How do I check that the image I have is the image you published?
items.a: SHA256SUMS carries the digests of the raw images and a minisign signature covers that file. Verify the signature first, then the digest against the raw image rather than against the compressed download.

privacy.lede: This site collects nothing. The detail below exists so that you do not have to take that on trust.

sections.body: One entry in your browser's localStorage, named eos-theme, holding the string light or dark. It never leaves your device, is never read by the project, and the site works correctly when it is absent or when storage is blocked entirely.

sections.h: What this site does not do
sections.body: No cookies. No analytics. No trackers, tag managers or advertising. No fonts, scripts, stylesheets or images loaded from a third-party host: everything a page needs is served from the same origin as the page.

The pages are served by GitLab Pages. Like any web server, that host processes your request, which includes your address and user agent, under its own operator's policy. The project has no access to those logs and does not receive them.
Links to GitLab, GitHub and Redox OS leave this site. From the moment you follow one, that operator's privacy policy applies and this one does not.

The support page composes a link; it transmits nothing. When you follow that link you are on GitLab, and GitLab's terms and privacy policy apply. Issues created there are public, including anything pasted into them.
Questions about this policy go to the maintainer address in the security policy. This page carries a review date; a material change moves that date and appears in the site repository's history.

terms.lede: The software is AGPL-3.0-or-later. This page states what that means in practice, and what it explicitly does not promise.

sections.body: E-OS as a whole is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 or later. Substantial parts derive from Redox OS and remain under the MIT licence, and individual files keep their own headers where they carry one. The AGPL governs E-OS's own contributions and the distribution of the combined work.

The software is provided without warranty of any kind, as the licence states. That is not a formality here: nothing has been booted on physical hardware, no third party has audited it, and it is maintained by one person.

Documentation and project information. It is not an offer, not a contract and not a support agreement. The response targets quoted on the support and security pages are stated targets from a single maintainer.

Read it, quote it, link to it; it is published under the same licence as the project. If you quote a measurement from it, quote the date with it — the numbers here are measurements, and measurements go stale.

Pages state what was measured and when. Where something has not been verified, the page says so instead of leaving it out. If you find a claim here that is not true, that is a defect and a ticket is the right response to it.
There is no legal entity behind E-OS and no jurisdiction is asserted. The limitation of liability is the one in the AGPL, and nothing on this site adds to it or takes anything away from it.

trademarks.lede: Redox OS is somebody else's trademark. E-OS is a downstream distribution, not official Redox OS software, and this page states the difference precisely.

sections.body: The Redox OS trademark — the name, the logo and the associated marks — belongs to the Redox OS nonprofit and is governed by their trademark policy, which took effect on 3 December 2025. E-OS follows that policy, and where this page and that policy differ, that policy governs.

sections.h: How E-OS refers to Redox OS
sections.body: Descriptively, to say what E-OS is built on. E-OS is third-party software for the Redox OS operating system. It does not use the Redox OS name or logo in a way that suggests official status, endorsement or sponsorship, and it does not alter the logo or fold it into a mark of its own.
Official Redox OS software may use the redox-os- package namespace and the org.redox_os. reverse-DNS prefix. E-OS is not official Redox OS software and uses neither.

E-OS, and the Crimson naming of the desktop, are the project's own. The NOTICE file reserves them; there is no registered mark and no legal entity to hold one. Use the name to refer to this project, and do not use it in a way that suggests a fork or a rebuild is the same software.

The COSMIC applications and icon themes are System76's. NetSurf belongs to the NetSurf developers. Rust and Cargo are the Rust Foundation's. Naming them here is descriptive use and implies no endorsement in either direction.

rules.h2: What you may and may not do
rules.intro: Summarised from the upstream policy and from how E-OS reads it. The full text is linked below and takes precedence over this summary.
items: You may say that your project runs on, extends or derives from E-OS, and that E-OS is a Redox OS downstream.
You may reproduce this documentation under the project's licence, including the names in it.
You may not imply that the Redox OS nonprofit endorses E-OS, or that E-OS is official Redox OS software. It is neither.
You may not use the Redox OS logo modified, or as part of another mark, without written permission from the Redox OS nonprofit.
You may not use the Redox OS trademark on merchandise for commercial purposes without their authorisation.
If you fork E-OS and change it, do not present the result as E-OS. Rename it, as you would with any distribution.

aboutEos.lede: Who publishes this site, under what licence, and what E-OS is in relation to Redox OS.

sections.body: E-OS is an independent open-source project maintained by one person. There is no company, no legal entity, no registered address and no funding. The copyright line reads "Damian (Gh0s777tt) and the E-OS contributors".

E-OS is a downstream distribution derived from Redox OS, the Rust microkernel operating system created by Jeremy Soller and the Redox OS community. The kernel, relibc, RedoxFS, the driver stack and the cookbook build system originate there and remain under the MIT licence.

None, formally. E-OS is not endorsed by, affiliated with or a product of the Redox OS project. It tracks upstream through pinned revisions and carries its patches in forks that are kept rebasable, so that the relationship stays a technical one.
Static pages generated from the project's own documents and build configuration, hosted on GitLab Pages. Its source is a separate repository under the same licence as the project.
The maintainer address in the security policy is the contact for everything: security reports, legal questions and press. There is no other channel and no press office.
